chunks: Ali ibn Ibrahim, from al-Mukhtar ibn Muhammad ibn al-Mukhtar al-Hamdani, and Muhammad ibn al-Hasan, from Abdullah ibn al-Hasan al-Alawi, all together from al-Fatah ibn Yazid al-Jurjani, from Abu al-Hasan (peace be upon him), who said:

I heard him saying: He is al-Latif (the Subtle), al-Khabir (the Aware), al-Sami' (the Hearing), al-Basir (the Seeing), al-Wahid (the One), al-Ahad (the Absolute One), al-Samad (the Self-Sufficient). He did not beget, nor was He begotten, and there is none equal to Him. Had He been as the anthropomorphists claim, the Creator would not be distinguished from the created, nor the Originator from the originated. But He is the Originator — there is a clear distinction between the One who shaped it, gave it form, and brought it into being, since nothing resembles Him, nor does He resemble anything.

I said: Indeed, may God make me your ransom! But you said al-Ahad al-Samad, and you said nothing resembles Him; yet God is one (wahid) and the human being is one (wahid). Has not the oneness (wahidaniyya) become similar?

He said: O Fatah! You have stated an impossibility — may God keep you firm! Indeed, resemblance is in meanings, not in names. As for names, they are one and the same, pointing to the named. This is because the human being, even if called 'one', is told he is a single body — not two. Yet the human being himself is not truly one, because his limbs are different and his colours are different; and one whose colours differ is not truly one. He is a collection of divided parts that are not equal: his blood is other than his flesh, his flesh other than his blood, his sinews other than his veins, his hair other than his skin, his darkness other than his whiteness. And so it is with all of creation.

The human being is one in name, yet there is no other one like him in meaning. But God — Glorified is His Majesty — He is One, there is no other one like Him; no difference in Him, no variation, no increase, no decrease. As for the human being: he is the created, the fashioned, the composed from different parts and diverse substances — except that in their gathering together he is one thing.

I said: May I be made your ransom — you have relieved me, may God relieve you! Now your saying 'al-Latif al-Khabir' — explain it to me as you explained al-Wahid (the One), for I know that His subtlety is contrary to the subtlety of His creation — yet I wish that you would elaborate on this for me.

So he said: O Fatah, we call Him al-Latif only because of His subtle creation and His knowledge of subtle things. Do you not see — may God grant you success and make you steadfast — the traces of His craftsmanship in delicate plants and in the subtle creatures, and the tiny animals: the mosquitoes and the gnats and what is even smaller than them — things that eyes can barely perceive, and whose male can barely even be distinguished from female, and the newborn from the aged, because of their smallness?

So when we saw the smallness of that in its subtlety — its instinctive guidance toward mating, flight from death, gathering what is beneficial for it, what is in the depths of the seas, what is in the bark of trees, the wastelands and barren deserts, and the mutual understanding between some of them and others through their language, and what their offspring understand from them, and their carrying food to them — then the composition of their colors: red with yellow, and white with red — and that which our eyes can barely perceive because of the smallness of their form — our eyes cannot see them, nor can our hands touch them — we recognized that the Creator of this creation is Subtle (Latif): He was subtle in creating what we have named, without manipulation, without instrument, without means. And every maker of something makes from something — but God, the Creator, the Subtle, the Majestic, He created and fashioned from nothing.

key_terms.التَّشْبِيهُ: Resemblance, anthropomorphism; the theological position that God's attributes resemble creation's attributes, refuted in this hadith
key_terms.الصَّمَدُ: al-Samad — the Self-Sufficient, the one upon whom all depend but who depends on nothing; key divine attribute from Quran 112:2
key_terms.اللَّطِيفُ: al-Latif — the Subtle, the Gentle; here interpreted as God's knowledge of the finest details of creation and His ability to create the most minute things
key_terms.الْمُشَبِّهَةُ: The anthropomorphists — those who liken God to creation in attributes or form; a theological sect opposed by Imami Shia scholars
key_terms.الْمُنْشِئُ: The Originator — the One who brings things into existence from nothing; contrasted with the created (al-munsha')
key_terms.الْوَحْدَانِيَّةُ: Oneness, divine unity — the attribute of being absolutely one; the Imam distinguishes God's real oneness from nominal human 'oneness'

ai.seo_question: How does Imam al-Ridha explain the difference between God's oneness and human oneness?
ai.summary: In this profound theological dialogue, Fatah ibn Yazid al-Jurjani narrates his encounter with Imam al-Ridha (AS) in which the Imam recites a divine glorification drawn from Surah al-Ikhlas (112), then explains two of God's attributes: al-Wahid (the One) and al-Latif (the Subtle). Responding to Fatah's question about why the word 'one' (wahid) applies both to God and to humans, the Imam distinguishes sharply between nominal identity (the same word) and real meaning: a human 'one' is a composite of heterogeneous parts, while God's oneness is absolute, undivided, and without any gradation or variation. For the term al-Latif, the Imam refers to the intricacy and precision of God's creation — from microscopic insects barely distinguishable to the naked eye, to creatures in the depths of seas and bark of trees — arguing that only a Creator without instruments or material cause could produce such minute, self-aware, purposeful life. This hadith is a foundational text in Shia kalam (theology) for refuting anthropomorphism (tashbih) and affirming God's incomparability (tanzih).
